leads.why: settle credits the whole rise since sync to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). The sweep of this cycle covered protocol addresses only. Reflection and rebasing tokens are common on BNB Smart Chain, and yield that accrues to the PoolManager balance could be claimed by whoever triggers it between sync and settle.

attempts.answer: The ledger already holds the answer for rebases and reward claims, and this unit adds the reflection case. Public rebases: the staked tokens of five Olympus forks on Polygon and BNB Smart Chain (F-066), with payouts or claim mints of the surplus on record for sSAC, sLGNS and sATH (F-091). Reward claims paid to the holder: QI for the qiAVAX balance on Avalanche (F-060). Reflection: a caller that brackets its own transfer of PIT or ASS with sync and settle pays the whole fee and is credited the PoolManager's share of it, about two parts in a billion in the simulation of this cycle, so that route has no gain. No new token of the first two kinds was looked for in this cycle.

leads.question: In Bor's BlockSTM executor and its serial fallback, is the transient storage of a task ever copied into the state database that the next task reads, for example when results are merged in transaction order?
leads.why: This cycle confirmed the reset in StateDB.Prepare for every message. The merge step in core/blockstm was not read line by line, and a copy of the journal there would break A1.

attempts.answer: The merge step copies only persistent paths of the multi-version write set (cycle 11, statedb.go lines 295-305 and 693-702 in v2.11.1), and those files are unchanged in v2.11.2 and v2.12.0-beta. Transient storage is never copied into the state a later task reads.

leads.question: What is the function behind selector 0xed9ef524 in the code at 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000001010, and can an ordinary account call it?
leads.why: It is the only entry of the native token contract that this cycle could not name. The contract holds 6.9 billion POL and mirrors the native balance of every account.

leads.question: Among the tokens the PoolManager holds on these three chains, which change state for the sender when the PoolManager sends a zero amount transfer, for example a reward that is auto-claimed to the sender in a second token, a per-sender transfer cooldown, or a fee swap-back?
leads.why: take(X, to, 0) records no delta (src/PoolManager.sol:294, src/PoolManager.sol:369) and still makes the PoolManager call X.transfer(to, 0) (src/types/Currency.sol:73), so any account can trigger sender-side token logic in the PoolManager's name at no cost. A reward paid to the PoolManager in token R between sync(R) and settle is credited to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360). A cooldown that restarts on every transfer could block later takes of X for every pool. This narrows the open lead on balances that rise without a transfer to one concrete trigger.

attempts.answer: Covered for the 12 to 15 largest pooled tokens on BNB Smart Chain, Polygon and Avalanche, and for 248 tokens over all 21 chains. A zero amount transfer from the PoolManager changes sender state in one token: qiAVAX on Avalanche, where it runs Benqi reward accounting for the PoolManager, and the public claimReward(0, PoolManager) would pay 14.84 accrued QI to the PoolManager if the Comptroller held it (it holds 0.11 QI, so the claim pays nothing today). sAVAX rejects zero amount transfers. No token in the samples has a per sender cooldown, an automatic claim to the sender, a fee paid by the sender or a swap back. On BNB Smart Chain SPCXB emits a second event with a display amount and nothing else changes. On Polygon all twelve tokens log only Transfer. The samples do not cover every pooled token.

leads.question: Do any BNB Smart Chain validators still run a v1.7.x client with the opcode fusion interpreter, and from which block is a v1.8 client required?
leads.why: The BSC changelog says v1.8.0-alpha removed the superinstruction feature of pull 3395 entirely (pull 3759), which explains why master has no such code. The v1.7.1 and v1.7.3 notes list three fixes to fused opcodes, one for a wrong LT comparison. The public endpoint reports Geth/v1.8.2, and v1.8.2 is mandatory before Jenner on 2026-12-08. Until every validator has moved, blocks can still be produced by the fused interpreter. A divergence there is a consensus fault and was not tied to any PoolManager opcode pattern.

leads.question: Among the 66,554 token rows of the mainnet PoolManager, which tokens other than the 12 sampled have a rebase, reward claim or airdrop claim that any account can trigger for a holder, and what does one trigger pay to the PoolManager?
leads.why: Each such token lets the first caller book the payment through sync and settle. The sample found no paying trigger today, and the long tail is unchecked.

attempts.answer: Already recorded as F-041 and F-067, and the long tail was swept by other units since the lead was written: the assign sweep of cycle 5 ran 168,712 trials on Ethereum and marked 99 trials on 34 tokens where a call by an ordinary account raised the PoolManager balance at no cost to the caller, most of them open mint functions on tokens that I did not price, and the trigger sweep of cycle 6 called every selector of 845 priced Ethereum tokens with the PoolManager as argument and found no paying trigger beyond those two findings. Measured today at block 26,480,258: calculateInterest() of Interest Protocol raises the PoolManager balance by 3,892.69 USDI, and the AMPL balance is 16 base units. A trigger that needs arguments the sweeps did not try (a Merkle proof, a signed report) remains outside what was tested.

leads.question: On each other network, is there an address that answers balanceOf(PoolManager) from a ledger which a plain value transfer or a zero amount call from the PoolManager raises, as EntryPoint.balanceOf and WETH9 do on mainnet, and that also answers transfer(address,uint256) from the PoolManager by releasing native value or a pooled token, at a rate, unit or fee other than 1:1?
leads.why: On mainnet the two halves meet only in WETH9, where the rate is 1:1 and both legs are booked, and in EntryPoint, which cannot pay out. A predeploy with a deposit ledger, a transfer function and a different rate or unit would turn take(address(0), X, amount) with sync(X) and settle around it into a credit larger than the native debit.

attempts.answer: On the three chains the only address with both halves is the wrapped native token, which exchanges one for one. The EntryPoints and the PositionManager have a ledger or a balanceOf answer and no transfer(address,uint256). No precompile or system address answers either call as an inner call from the PoolManager. Application contracts outside the swept list were not examined.

leads.question: On which other networks can an account run code while msg.sender == tx.origin holds (EIP-7702 or a native batch or account abstraction transaction type), and which pooled tokens there guard a public rebase, reward push or mint with that check?
leads.why: The finding in this file needs only that check to fall. Networks with native account abstraction may have had this property since launch, and a rebasing or reward token with real liquidity there would make the amount material.

leads.question: Do the sweep results of the other units change when the call is made by the PoolManager address with a different transaction origin, using a small forwarder placed at the PoolManager address by state override, for every target that did not revert under plain eth_call and for every target that reverted with an origin or EOA message?
leads.why: With from set to the PoolManager a plain eth_call makes tx.origin equal to msg.sender. On mainnet that mode showed the OP Mainnet L1StandardBridge accepting a payout that it refuses in the real call shape, and it hid the aliased sender of portal deposits. A predeploy that treats an origin caller differently could be misfiled as safe or as unsafe.

leads.question: Do the second entry points of TUSD (0x8dd5fbCe2F6a956C3022bA3663759011Dd51e73E) and SNX (0xC011A72400E58ecD99Ee497CF89E3775d4bd732F) still forward transfer and balanceOf for the PoolManager's balance, and does a self transfer of any pooled token, take(X, PoolManager, amount), raise balanceOf(PoolManager)?
leads.why: The double entry clearance rests on the accounting argument and was not exercised on chain. A token whose self transfer credits the recipient without debiting the sender would give a free credit between sync and settle.

leads.question: How does the MegaETH sequencer order candidates inside a block (arrival order or priority fee), and are transactions that were skipped for a block-level limit placed ahead of newer arrivals in the next block?
leads.why: This decides whether one sender who fills the state growth budget each block delays other users by one block or can keep them out for as long as it pays.

attempts.answer: The order is not by priority fee. In 232 of 300 sampled blocks a transaction with a lower priority fee precedes one with a higher fee from another sender (525 of 3,316 neighbouring pairs). That fits arrival order per mini-block. Whether skipped transactions keep their place could not be established, because the sequencer's pool is closed source, the documentation is silent, and no block with a full state budget exists in 400,000 recent blocks to observe.

First half answered: the order inside a block is the order of the 10 ms mini-blocks, and the fee does not order transactions even inside one mini-block (44 of 324 neighbouring pairs from different senders have the later one paying more, in 21,400 consecutive mini-blocks). Second half still open: the public gateway delivered no pending transaction in 214 seconds, the FAQ says the pool cannot be inspected, and the only text on skipped transactions is an executor comment that they are typically put back in the pool. Their place there is unknown.

No new evidence. The executor and limiter code on mega-evm main is byte identical to v1.7.4, and the sequencer pool that decides where a skipped transaction goes is closed. The time order shown in cycle 7 stands.

leads.question: Are L1 deposit transactions placed before sequencer transactions in every MegaETH block, and what does the node do when a deposit itself brings the block's state growth counter to 1,000 while further deposits of the same L1 block remain?
leads.why: The block limiter applies the state growth test to deposits. If a later deposit can be skipped, the forced inclusion path that F-017 relies on has a gap, and a derivation mismatch would be an operator-level fault.

attempts.answer: Deposits sit at index 1 in 25 of 25 sampled deposit blocks, ahead of system and sequencer transactions. One L1 block can carry at most 20,000,000 gas of deposits (resourceConfig on the L1 SystemConfig), which pays for fewer than 900 new slots, so deposits alone cannot bring the counter to 1,000, and the transaction that reaches the limit is itself admitted. The forced inclusion route of F-017 has no gap from this limit.

leads.question: Which currencies outside the Monad token list, the Uniswap list and the documentation page have a balance at the Monad PoolManager? Enumerate currency0 and currency1 from the Initialize events and repeat the classification for issuer controls, second entry points and balances that change without transfers.
leads.why: The list checked covers 147 tokens. A token with two entry points or a rebasing balance outside that list was not looked at.

attempts.answer: Enumerated from Initialize logs since deployment: 19,402 pools, 11,268 token currencies, 8,375 with a balance. New holdings of size are ten wrapped stock tokens worth 7.9 million dollars, 40 cbBTC, 337 bridged WETH and 1.7 WBTC. The wrapped stock tokens and cbBTC carry pause, sanctions, freeze and burn rights and are added to F-015. No second entry point to a pooled balance and no mirror of the native balance was found. Balances that change without transfers are Aave and Neverland deposit tokens with at most 24,696 nWMON (about 300 dollars) and unwrapped stock tokens at dust size.

leads.question: Who holds the proxy admin of GHO (0x06ba20fb633cbf38b7acfdc243829fb5f897e19c) and of mUSD (0x685e7f8c9414bfa716b254b349153e2317929ac9), the owner of shMON (0x48a3267bcc4cf230e9bc4cae0c11eebdb9a6a687), BURNER_ROLE on syrupUSDC and the upgrade right on apxUSD, and does burn(address,uint256) on syrupUSDC and apxUSD need an allowance from the account?
leads.why: This decides whether an issuer action against the PoolManager address is a pause that can be undone or a loss, for about 6.2 million units of dollar tokens and 269,214 shMON.

leads.question: What is NUM_KV_BUCKETS in the SALT repository, and can entries for a chosen bucket be found without brute force given the fixed-seed hash?
leads.why: The cost estimate for inflating one bucket assumes the attacker can place entries at will. The estimate also bounds a combined case in which the sequencer censors a user and the user's forced removal through L1, which an earlier lead puts at 20 million gas, needs a new slot in an inflated bucket.

leads.question: Obtain the full BlockSec report for MegaEVM and the Runtime Verification report for Monad execution and read the notes on fixed gas calls, sender balance taint and reserve balance proofs.
leads.why: Only the index of the BlockSec report and a search extract of the Runtime Verification report were read. A note could describe a behaviour of value calls that matters for native payouts.

leads.question: Does a run of N transactions that each create 1,000 new state entries, submitted together from several accounts, close N consecutive MegaETH blocks for every transaction that arrives after the run, and what limits per sender or per block does the sequencer's pending pool apply to such a run?
leads.why: The finding assumes the sender must win the first place in every block. Under arrival order a queued run would hold that place for N blocks at 0.0000226 ETH each, which is about 1.95 ETH for a day in which no PoolManager withdrawal is included. That would move the finding from a delay inside one block to blocked liquidity operations.

attempts.answer: Not observed and not excluded. Blocks are not ordered by fee, so under arrival order a queue of N filling transactions from several accounts would hold N blocks and delay later arrivals by N seconds at about 0.0000226 ETH per second. The only documented pool limit is 500 pending transactions per account. The delay is bounded by the queue length at arrival and does not reach L1 deposits, which are placed first. F-042 is updated with this bound and stays low.

Not observed and not excluded. Under the time order shown above a run of N filling transactions would hold N blocks if skipped transactions keep their place, at 0.0000226 ETH per block. The only documented pool limit remains 500 pending transactions per account. New for the way out: a forced transaction from L1 is limited to 1,000,000 gas, a normal removal fits, and the route can be closed per position by growing a SALT bucket (first finding of this file).

Not observed and not excluded. The bound of F-062 stands: N fillers close at most N blocks at about 0.0000226 ETH each, at the 1,000,000 wei base fee read on 2026-11-25, and only if skipped transactions keep their place. No fork is scheduled that changes the limit.

leads.question: Is there a mainnet block in which a transaction with 1,000 new state entries is followed by further sequencer transactions in the same block? Search for transactions near 22.5 million gas that write about 1,000 fresh slots and read their position in the block.
leads.why: The block-level skip is confirmed in the reference limiter and the specification and was not observed on chain. One counterexample would show that the live sequencer does not apply the block limit as written, and one positive example would confirm it.

attempts.answer: No example in either direction. Headers of blocks 32,206,276 to 32,606,276 were read. 359 blocks exceed 20 million gas. The 30 transactions above 12 million gas in blocks of 20 to 80 million gas were traced, and the largest state growth is 27 entries. The heavy transactions are contract deployments. Blocks before 32,206,276 were not scanned.

No example in either direction. A counterexample cannot pass validation: block/executor.rs applies pre_execution_check to every transaction, and the stateless validator pins the same code at v1.7.3, so a block with a transaction after the limit was reached is invalid. A positive example needs a transaction near 1,000 new entries, and block gas does not find one: a scan of gasUsedRatio by eth_feeHistory over about 4.4 million blocks between 2,000,000 and 28,114,829 found 13,609 blocks at or above 22.5 million gas, far too many to trace, and the scan was stopped because the endpoint slowed to one batch per minute. An index of state growth per transaction would be needed.

Not attempted again. Without an index of state growth per transaction, finding a transaction with 1,000 new entries needs per-transaction traces over millions of blocks. The source argument from cycle 7 stands: a counterexample would fail stateless validation.

leads.question: Which currencies appear in pools of the HyperEVM PoolManager? The public RPC limits eth_getLogs to 1,000 blocks, so the Initialize events of about 52 million blocks need an archive node or an indexer. For each currency, is it rebasing, does it have a second entry point, or is it a contract whose balanceOf can rise without a transfer?
leads.why: This cycle checked balances of 16 known tokens by hand and found the stHYPE and wstHYPE pair by reading issuer docs. A full list would show whether a pool already uses the stHYPE face or another token of this kind.

attempts.answer: The archive endpoint https://rpc.purroofgroup.com serves eth_getLogs over 100,000 blocks, which made a full list possible. 344 pools, 308 currencies, 53 hooks since block 45,998,366. For 306 of 307 ERC-20 currencies the PoolManager balance equals its Transfer logs. The exception is a test token without logs. No Transfer log naming the PoolManager comes from a contract outside the list, so no pooled token has a second entry point. stHYPE and wstHYPE are in no pool. Value held is small: 11.38 HYPE, 14.78 WHYPE, 997.75 USDC and test or launch tokens.

leads.question: What does the Overseer implementation at 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c do in mint, burnAndRedeemIfPossible and redeem: can any of them call stHYPE.syncSupply, and how is getNewSupply computed from read precompiles while HYPE is in flight between HyperCore and the EVM?
leads.why: The contract is not verified on Sourcify. If a public function can trigger syncSupply with a supply below the current one, for example while funds are in flight and the precompiles under-report, the loss shift between the stHYPE and wstHYPE ids described in the finding would no longer need the rebaser.

attempts.answer: Measured on the official node inside one eth_call from a real holder's address: mint and burnAndRedeemIfPossible change the stHYPE supply by exactly the amount minted or burned and leave balancePerShare, syncStart, syncEnd and rewardsToSync unchanged, so neither calls syncSupply. redeem reverted for the test caller and is left as a low lead. The implementation is still unverified. No pool holds stHYPE or wstHYPE.

leads.question: How does HyperCore bind an AQAv2 treasury address to a token: does the named address have to send an EVM transaction or sign a message, and can the treasury deployer change the address after activation? The treasury address for USDC has no HyperCore account and no stake.
leads.why: This is the remaining open link of F-020 and of leads L-065, L-074 and L-116. If no consent is needed, two staked deployers and a validator vote can make HyperCore send transfers from the PoolManager.

attempts.answer: The treasury address does not have to send an EVM transaction, sign a HyperCore action or hold a HyperCore account. Its first transaction (nonce 0, block 37,597,803) is an unsigned system transaction that moved 2,001 USDC out of it, it held 0 HYPE before, and the info API reports userExists false and userHasSentTx false. The designation is separate from the authorizeAqav2Role action, which carries no address and was sent by the staking account 0x4E5319dEb1072B01439EE674db5C321d11fd96F8. Whether the deployer can change the address after activation is still unknown and is a new lead. F-020 is re-reported with this evidence.

leads.question: On HyperEVM testnet, send two transactions that land in one block: the first calls PoolManager.sync on a token and nothing else, the second reads the synced currency slot through exttload. Does the validator node return zero in the second?
leads.why: It would test assumption A1 on the closed validator binary directly. The present clearance rests on the archive client reproducing every block header. The test needs transactions, which this review does not send.

leads.question: Does a complete swap through unlock, with settlement in ERC-6909 claims, fit in the 200,000 gas of a linked contract's system transaction, and in which order does HyperCore place several system transactions in one block?
leads.why: It decides how useful the first position of a block is to an account that links its own contract, and so whether the ordering finding deserves more than low.

leads.question: What does MRB stand for, and has Hyperliquid stated whether further repricing or per block resource limits are planned? The change is visible in the archive client release of 10 November 2026 and not in the HyperEVM docs.
leads.why: A change of execution rules with one day of public notice is a hazard for hooks and routers that budget gas tightly. A statement of intent would show whether opcode prices that core depends on could change the same way.

leads.question: What bounds the gasLimit of a sendToEvmWithData action, is the gas of the resulting coreReceiveWithData system transaction left out of the block total like other system transactions, and where in the block is it placed?
leads.why: The exchange API lets the sender of this HyperCore action choose a gas limit and a data payload for a call into a linked contract, and anyone can link a contract of their own. If the limit is large, the 200,000 gas bound in the ordering finding does not hold, and uncounted execution ahead of signed transactions could also lengthen blocks. Neither the cycle 1 state nor the cycle 2 research file mentions this action.

attempts.answer: The documentation gives sendToEvmWithData a gasLimit field and no maximum. On chain all 60 coreReceiveWithData system transactions in 4,725 blocks carry 200,000 gas, target the CoreDepositWallet and sit before the signed transactions, like every other system transaction (1,927 of 1,927). The archive client leaves the gas of system transactions out of the block total (executor.rs lines 225 to 227). I saw no transaction with another gas value, so the bound is not established. A testnet action with a larger gasLimit would settle it.

The node now bounds it. The API announcements channel stated on 2026-11-19 that from the next network upgrade sendToEvmWithData consumes at most 200k gas even if a higher gas limit is passed, and the next upgrade was announced for about 09:30 UTC on 2026-11-21. In blocks 52,048,026 to 52,052,025 all 336 coreReceiveWithData system transactions carry 200,000 gas, target the CoreDepositWallet and sit before the signed transactions, as do all 3,179 system transactions of the sample. Their gas is left out of the block total in the archive client (executor.rs lines 224 to 227). The announcement implies that a larger limit was honoured before the upgrade. I saw no such transaction.

leads.question: Is there a past HyperEVM block in which one transaction called PoolManager.sync on an ERC-20 without a settle and a later transaction of the same block made a native settle with value that succeeded?
leads.why: Such a pair is a read only test of assumption A1 against the validator itself: with leaked transient storage the second transaction would revert with NonzeroNativeValue (src/PoolManager.sol:356). It needs an archive node or an indexer with traces, since sync emits no event and the public RPC limits eth_getLogs to 1,000 blocks.

attempts.answer: No such block exists: a call trace of all 2,782 PoolManager transactions finds no successful transaction that ends with an ERC-20 synced, so no later native settle could meet a leaked sync. The transaction boundary of transient storage was tested directly on the three endpoints in earlier cycles.

leads.question: Does Overseer.redeem(uint256) or any other public function of the unverified Overseer implementation at 0x2b8698dd4b8addf7ddcabc46c6aedafe5a70b11c change stHYPE totalSupplyRaw or totalShares out of proportion inside one transaction?
leads.why: A simulation in this check showed that public mint and burnAndRedeemIfPossible leave a holder's stHYPE balance unchanged. redeem and the remaining selectors of the 24,255 byte implementation were not tried. A public call that moves the rate would let an ordinary account open a sync window on the stHYPE id and be credited the rise, once the PoolManager holds stHYPE.

leads.question: Has any source hash been added to the TxBlacklist at 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727, which accounts are operators, and which commit of the okx/optimism submodule does the mainnet sequencer build pin?
leads.why: The high finding on voided deposits rests on source at tag xlayer/v0.1.7 and on the deployed contract. An indexer with full log access can show whether the rule has been used and against whom. The public endpoint limits eth_getLogs to 100 blocks.

attempts.answer: Operator only hazard. I read the logs of the contract with eth_getLogs in windows of 100 blocks for blocks 66,955,423 to 67,242,822 (2026-08-06 10:24 UTC) and blocks 75,407,023 (2026-11-08 22:14 UTC) to 76,607,000 (2026-11-22 19:33 UTC), which is 15 percent of the range since its creation. The second range starts before the date by which operators had to run the release that contains the deposit blacklist rule (10 November 2026). The public endpoints limit the request rate, so blocks 67,242,823 to 75,407,022 were not read. The creation block 66,955,423 (3 August 2026) holds four logs: Upgraded, OwnershipTransferred to 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa, Initialized and AdminChanged. The ranges that were read hold no other log. The OKLink page https://www.oklink.com/x-layer/address/0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 shows no transaction records for the contract. The owner of the contract and of its proxy admin is still 0x6EE7bDA7aF04F61ccf93aB4b8Db2289aBe76C6aa. Which commit of the okx/optimism submodule the mainnet sequencer runs could not be read: the endpoint reports reth/v2.3.0-f60420a with xlayer/v0.0.7 and the submodule commit is not visible through raw file access.

Operator only hazard. No source hash is listed and no operator is appointed at block 76,668,710 (2026-11-23): the storage trie of 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727 has exactly four leaves (implementation, admin, owner, initialized flag), walked from the storage root and tied to the state root of that block from rpc.xlayer.tech. An entry added and later removed inside the unread log range would not show. The commit of the okx/optimism submodule in the sequencer build cannot be read from chain. The repository publishes tags named xlayer-dep with a commit hash, and at the newest one, a492b62bbecbdcf3be90719e042c9abca47c8cc6, the six consensus files (alloy-op-evm lib.rs, the blacklist and gasless contract files, op-revm handler.rs, evm.rs and precompiles.rs) are byte identical to tag xlayer/v0.1.7.

leads.question: Can any error that the OKX handler raises for a non-deposit transaction occur after contract code has run in that transaction, given that its catch_error leaves the journal in place?
leads.why: The executor aborts the block on such an error, and the builder skips the transaction and reuses the same EVM. If code could run before the error, transient storage written by the rejected transaction, such as a synced currency in the PoolManager, would be visible to the next transaction the builder simulates, and the builder would produce a block that validators reject.

leads.question: Which tokens held by the X Layer PoolManager besides USDT0, USDC, Wrapped OKB and the bridged WETH answer at more than one address or change balances without a transfer?
leads.why: The sweep covered system contracts and the largest holdings. A token with two entry points or a rebasing balance would be a second face of one balance (A2, A3).

leads.question: Does every future CELO token implementation keep the property that the token address calls no contract outside Governance control?
leads.why: The transfer precompile accepts a DELEGATECALL from any contract that the token address calls, because the caller field is inherited. A token upgrade that adds a callback to a recipient or to a registered hook would let that callee move native CELO from any account, including the PoolManager. The upgrade itself needs Governance.

leads.question: Which op-reth commit does the OP Mainnet sequencer run, given that the public endpoint reports op-reth/v0.0.0-dev-unknown, and does it include the reth trie fix from pull request 28264 and the op-revm error path that discards a failed transaction's journal?
leads.why: Every source based clearance for OP Mainnet in this cycle rests on the commit that Unichain, Ink and Soneium report. The largest OP Stack balances outside Base sit on this chain.

leads.question: In the World Chain node, does the parallel validation path for flashblocks with block access lists execute each transaction on its own journal, and is a transaction whose result disagrees with the access list re-executed from clean transient storage?
leads.why: Assumption A1 names parallel execution with speculative state as a way for an unlock flag or a delta to reach another execution. The sequential path was read and is safe. The parallel path was not read to the end.

attempts.answer: At world-chain v2.8.2 the parallel flashblock validation builds a new State and a new EVM instance for every transaction and executes it without commit, so each transaction has its own journal and an empty transient map. The results are committed in index order and the access list hash, receipts root, state root and block hash must match the sequencer's, otherwise the flashblock is rejected with an error. No re-execution with shared transient state exists in that file.

leads.question: reth v2.10.0 names a new execution engine, evm2, in its SDK changes, and the Base workspace has a crate base-common-evm2. When a chain in this unit moves block execution from revm to that engine, do TSTORE rollback on revert, clearing at transaction end, rollback of precompile state on a failed frame, and calls to addresses without code keep the behaviour read in this cycle?
leads.why: All opcode and transient storage clearances of this cycle were read from revm. A second engine needs the same reading before it produces blocks.

attempts.answer: No chain of the unit runs evm2. All seven endpoints report the client builds of cycle 2, and the Base crate base-common-evm2 is documented as not wired into the node. The question is open again when a release moves block execution to that engine.

leads.question: Does Base plan a third B20 variant byte, and at the fork that defines it, can any address that was a plain account without code before the fork already hold ERC-6909 claims or pool state in the PoolManager under its currency id?
leads.why: Before a variant is defined its addresses accept transfer calls silently. This cycle found no way to hold credit in such an id, and the check should be repeated against the fork's token logic.

leads.question: Which tokens held by the PoolManager on Base and OP Mainnet raise a holder's balance through a call that any account can make, such as a rebase payout or a claim on behalf of the holder? The PoolManager holds 112.55 USD+ on Base, a token that rebases for every holder, and the caller of its payout function was not read.
leads.why: A caller who runs sync, the trigger and settle in one transaction is credited the whole increase on the PoolManager balance (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288 and 349-364). Cycle 1 raised this for stETH on Ethereum. The balances found here are small, and a larger rebasing or reward token would make it a loss of yield for LPs.

attempts.answer: No token was found. The trigger probe called 70 public functions on each of 1,594 tokens on OP Mainnet and 9,108 on Base and no balance of the PoolManager changed. The USD+ payout on Base is not public: changeSupply needs the exchanger and payout() on the exchange reverts for an account without a role. The PoolManager holds 112.37 USD+. The Base list covers tokens that moved in one day, and triggers that live on a second contract are outside the probe.

leads.question: Do the deployed Universal Router and PositionManager on these chains accept a predeploy such as L2ToL1MessagePasser or an EntryPoint as the recipient of a native payout, and how did 0.0588 ETH reach the Base PoolManager address on Ethereum?
leads.why: The stranding finding of this cycle needs a user facing path to matter. A router that filters recipients would close it, and the L1 balance may show that it has already happened.

leads.question: What did the v1.18.2 item 'EVM call input hardening' and the v1.18.4 'fix for EVM execution' change in evm2 or in Tempo's handler, is the evm2 JIT backend enabled in the mainnet build, and does the PoolManager bytecode give the same results under the interpreter and the JIT for its call, return data and transient storage sequences?
leads.why: Tempo runs a new interpreter that received two execution fixes in November 2026 without a public description. The PoolManager's payout check reads return data size and memory right after a CALL, and its accounting lives in transient storage. A defect in either area would be specific to this network.

attempts.answer: Answered in part. The jit feature is optional at the mainnet commit 697ea97 and is absent from the default features and from the release Dockerfile, so the stock build runs the evm2 interpreter only. I could not confirm what each validator builds. Through the deployed PoolManager bytecode, 256 swaps and 288 paid adds gave the amounts of the source formulas, and 1,008 arithmetic opcode cases matched. The commits behind the v1.18.2 and v1.18.4 notes remain unidentified, because the commit history could not be read from this environment.

Both changes are identified. v1.18.2 moved from revm 43.0.3 to evm2 with a patch that passes call input as a borrowed range of the caller's memory; at the mainnet revision 66687c18 the range is resolved through the caller frame on each read. v1.18.4 changed two files with identical dependencies: the precompile provider and the T14 account marker instruction now check that the remaining gas covers the input cost before they copy the borrowed input. Neither touches return data or transient storage handling. A 32 case differential on nested calls with overlapping input and output ranges matched revm byte for byte. The jit feature is outside the default build (cycle 4). Not confirmed: the build features of each validator.

leads.question: Can the Universal Router deployments, the PositionManager or Permit2 on Tempo be made to call TIP403Registry.setReceivePolicy as themselves through any command, callback or subscriber path, and do they take TIP-20 payouts to themselves before forwarding?
leads.why: Anyone who can make a forwarding contract set its own receive policy can name themselves recovery authority. Every later TIP-20 payout from the PoolManager to that contract would then be credited to ReceivePolicyGuard and be claimable by the attacker. All policies were unset at block 50,287,321.

attempts.answer: No. The setReceivePolicy selector 0xdda03d86 is absent from the bytecode of the PositionManager, both Universal Routers and Permit2, and none of them forwards caller supplied calldata to an address other than their immutable position managers, the PoolManager, tokens and subscribers with fixed selectors. Their receive policies are unset at block 50,363,131. The routers do take TIP-20 payouts to themselves before forwarding, and those payouts are credited normally.

leads.question: Do the Universal Router and PositionManager on Arc call sync(address(0)) before a native settle, and how do they treat a pool or a route that names both address(0) and 0x3600?
leads.why: sync needs no unlock, and three EntryPoint contracts are deployed on Arc. An earlier user operation in the same bundle can leave 0x3600 synced, after which a native settle without a fresh sync reverts with NonzeroNativeValue. The bundler collects the gas of the failed operation.

attempts.answer: Both routers and the PositionManager on Arc call sync(address(0)) before a native settle. With sync(0x3600) or sync(EURC) left by an earlier call in the same transaction, a native SETTLE through each of the three contracts succeeds at block 32,662,000, while a direct settle with value reverts with NonzeroNativeValue. The contracts treat address(0) and 0x3600 as unrelated currencies, and their wrapped native immutable is a contract that always reverts.

leads.question: Which arc-node release do mainnet validators run behind the client string arc/v1, is Zero8 active, and does that release contain the ruint correction listed for v0.8.0?
leads.why: All source claims for Arc in this cycle rest on the main branch. The ruint note concerns shift and overflow handling in EVM arithmetic, which the pool math depends on.

attempts.answer: Zero7 and Zero8 are active on mainnet since 1789052400 (2026-09-10) and require v0.8.0 or later; v0.8.0 lists the ruint correction for overflow flags and shift amounts, and every v0.8.x tag pins ruint 1.20.0 and revm-interpreter 35.0.1. Which exact release each validator runs is not published, but every release that can follow the chain has the same arithmetic.

leads.question: Is a TIP-20 amount sent by plain transfer to the FeeManager, StablecoinDEX or TIP20ChannelReserve address recoverable by anyone, for example through a reserve sync in the Fee AMM or the exchange?
leads.why: It decides whether a mistaken payout from the PoolManager to these addresses is lost or can be collected by the next caller of those precompiles.

leads.question: For each chain, name every feature that runs caller-chosen code against live state with a transient storage map other than the one of the surrounding transaction: Tempo zone contracts and the T14 ConfigurableAccount, Base Transactions of type 0x79, Stylus host calls and retryable redeems on the Arbitrum family, coreReceiveWithData system transactions on HyperEVM, PBH bundles on World Chain, the fee currency calls on Celo, and any keyless deploy, simulation or sandbox precompile. For each one, can an ordinary contract start it from inside a call, does the inner run begin with an empty or a copied transient map, and are its storage and balance writes kept?
leads.why: This is the one chain property that turns the settlement code into a direct loss for every pool. sync needs no lock and keeps the reserves in transient storage (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288). If an inner run with an empty map can pay tokens in, settle and mint a claim (src/PoolManager.sol:349-364, 322-329) and its writes are kept, the outer settle credits the same tokens a second time. If the inner run starts from a copy and drops its transient writes, a take inside it leaves no debit (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297). The settlement unit raised the question and no network unit answered it except for MegaETH, where the critic found that the sandbox starts only at depth zero.

attempts.answer: Stylus host calls: an ordinary contract can start them, they share the transient map of the transaction, and their writes are kept like any other call. Retryable redeems: an ordinary contract can request one inside a call through ArbRetryableTx.redeem, the redeem does not run inside that call, and it starts as a separate transaction with an empty map after the requesting transaction has ended. Node interface simulations run only in RPC calls. No feature gives an inner run with its own map inside a running transaction.

leads.question: On each client, is there any way for a call frame to carry a nonzero CALLVALUE while the caller's balance does not fall by the same amount in the same journal? Check the system caller rule (go-ethereum master and BNB Smart Chain master skip the balance check and the transfer when the caller is 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe, read by the critic at core/vm/evm.go lines 311 to 347 of bnb-chain/bsc; Bor v2.11.0 does not), deposit transactions with a mint field on the OP Stack chains including the custom gas token chains, retryable tickets and unsigned L1 messages on the Arbitrum family, gasless transactions on X Layer, the sandbox signer on MegaETH, system transactions on HyperEVM, and fee payer or sponsored transactions on Tempo and Arc. Which sender addresses reach those paths and can any of them enter contract code that an ordinary account chose?
leads.why: A native credit is msg.value and nothing else (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354). The code never compares it with a balance change, so a frame that reports value it did not pay receives a native credit for free and can take every native balance and, through pools, other tokens. Assumption A3 lists the unit of msg.value and the faces of the native asset and does not list this. The established L1 unit recorded the system caller rule on BNB Smart Chain with relevance none and no unit asked the question for the other clients.

attempts.answer: Every value frame is backed by a balance debit on all three live nodes. The system caller exemption is in the fork source and is disabled for Arbitrum chains below Amsterdam. Deposits create no call frame, retryables pay their call value from an escrow funded by the parent chain deposit, and unsigned messages spend the aliased sender's balance. A probe with code placed at the system address confirmed the balance check on each chain. A low priority lead covers the Amsterdam version.

leads.question: Does the source text satisfy every statement the repository makes about itself in the files no unit has replayed? Replay by reading or by transcription: test/libraries/TickMath.t.sol, SqrtPriceMath.t.sol, SwapMath.t.sol, FullMath.t.sol, BitMath.t.sol, UnsafeMath.t.sol, StateLibrary.t.sol and Lock.t.sol, test/types/Currency.t.sol (the transfer cases from line 122 on), test/Tick.t.sol, test/DynamicFees.t.sol, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol, test/SkipCallsTestHook.t.sol, test/PoolManager.swap.t.sol, test/Extsload.t.sol, test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.t.sol and the hook and initialize cases of test/PoolManager.t.sol. Then compare every NatSpec sentence in src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol, IProtocolFees.sol and IHooks.sol with the function it describes, and compare src/PoolManager.sol with the two other implementations of the same interface inside this repository, src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol and src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol, function by function.
leads.why: The owner states that this build carries a planted weakness and has ruled out comparison with other copies. The tests, the interface comments and the test doubles in this repository are then the only reference for intended behaviour. Cycle 1 found four places where the source departs from them (F-006), two of them in Pool.swap, and lead L-118 is still open with the files listed here unread. A fifth departure in a path that moves funds would be the planted item or would point at it.

attempts.answer: The part assigned to this unit is answered and found no new departure with a fund effect. Replayed and satisfied by the source text: test/PoolManager.t.sol (all numbers on a transcription, all 27 expectRevert cases and the hook and initialize cases by reading), test/PoolManager.swap.t.sol (differential against the v3 bytecode fixture in a Python EVM interpreter), test/DynamicFees.t.sol, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol, test/SkipCallsTestHook.t.sol, test/Extsload.t.sol, test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.t.sol and the transfer cases of test/types/Currency.t.sol. Every NatSpec sentence of IPoolManager.sol, IProtocolFees.sol and IHooks.sol was compared with its function, and six more wording differences without fund effect are recorded in this unit's finding. src/PoolManager.sol was read function by function against src/test/ProxyPoolManager.sol and src/test/ProtocolFeesImplementation.sol: the proxy adds noDelegateCall to unlock, take, settle, settleFor, mint and burn and emits Initialize after afterInitialize, and neither difference gives access to funds held by the PoolManager. Still open under this lead: the library test files it names (TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, FullMath, BitMath, UnsafeMath, StateLibrary, Lock and test/Tick.t.sol), which belong to the unit core-code-tests-replay-libraries, and the bytecode size and creation code hash recorded in snapshots/PoolManagerTest.json for test_bytecodeSize and test_initcodeHash, which need a compiler. The libraries unit of this cycle has filed a lead for that check.

leads.question: protocolFeeController is the zero address on these eleven chains. For each client, which frames can have msg.sender equal to address(0): the system calls of Tempo's block executor, HyperEVM system transactions whose sender the node accepts as any 20 bytes, the Celo fee currency debit and credit calls, Monad and MegaETH system senders, OP Stack upgrade deposits, and ArbOS internal transactions on Elysium? Can an ordinary account choose the target or the calldata of any of them?
leads.why: setProtocolFee and collectProtocolFees accept any caller that equals the stored controller (src/ProtocolFees.sol:35-36, 48). A caller that can appear as address(0) could set the protocol fee of every pool to the cap and withdraw what accrues. The cycle 1 critic recorded contradicting clearances on this point. Cycle 2 answered it for X Layer and Avalanche only.

leads.question: On which of these chains is EIP-7702 or a native batch transaction type active, so that code runs while msg.sender equals tx.origin, and which tokens held by the PoolManager there guard a public rebase, reward push or mint with that test? Start from the tokens already named: USD+ on Base, the aTokens on Arbitrum One and MegaETH, and any Ampleforth style token.
leads.why: The Ethereum unit confirmed that an ordinary account can call a guarded rebase from inside its own unlock callback and book the rise of balanceOf(PoolManager) as its payment (src/PoolManager.sol:358-364). No other unit tested which chains share that account model. Where one balance is read under two ids, as the HyperEVM unit found for stHYPE and wstHYPE, a rise booked under the rebasing id also removes the yield of pools in the other id, so the answer decides how far the Ethereum finding reaches.

leads.question: Does a distributor that pays holders on a third party's call owe anything to the PoolManager address on any chain? Check the Merkl distributor, Compound style claim functions, and any airdrop contract with a claim for an arbitrary account, for each of the ten largest token holdings of each PoolManager. What does one claim pay, in which token, and is that token the currency of any pool?
leads.why: A claim that any account can trigger raises a token balance of the PoolManager inside the caller's transaction. With sync before and settle after, the caller is credited the whole amount (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, 358-364). The PoolManager is among the largest holders of many tokens, so reward programs that pay by holding are likely to list it. The Ethereum unit checked three such triggers on mainnet and none on the other chains.

leads.question: Which tokens held by the PoolManager change state for the sender when the PoolManager sends a transfer of zero: a transfer cooldown per sender, a counter of transfers per block, a reward that is claimed to the sender, or a fee swap inside the token? The call costs nothing: take(token, anyRecipient, 0) inside an unlock.
leads.why: take with amount zero makes the PoolManager call transfer and owes nothing (src/PoolManager.sol:291-297, 368-369). A token that limits how often one sender may transfer would let any account use up that limit in every block and so stop every payout of that token to all pools, with no role and no cost beyond gas. The verifier of the established L1 unit asked this for three chains only.

leads.question: Repeat the special address sweep with a forwarding stub placed at the PoolManager address by state override and a different account as transaction sender. For which targets does the answer to empty calldata with value, transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address) or a hook selector differ from the answer to a top-level call from the PoolManager address?
leads.why: See the gap entry. The real calls are inner frames (src/types/Currency.sol:48, 73, 94 and src/libraries/Hooks.sol:134). A target that pays or credits the origin, or that accepts only contract callers, was tested in the one shape that cannot occur.

attempts.answer: Ethereum now has the stub sweep: 18 shapes on 95 addresses at block 26,480,192, with the PoolManager as inner frame and an unrelated origin. The results for precompiles and system contracts equal the plain call sweep of cycle 2, and the 69 added staking, bridge and infrastructure contracts give no credit that was not paid for.

leads.question: Through the Quoter listed in state/networks.json for each chain, quote an exact input and an exact output swap that crosses at least three initialized ticks in the largest pool, in both directions, and compare the amounts with a transcription of src/libraries/Pool.sol, SwapMath.sol and SqrtPriceMath.sol run on the pool state read through extsload at the same block. Do all 21 networks agree to the last unit?
leads.why: This runs the deployed PoolManager bytecode through each node's own execution path, including the compiled path on Monad, the evm2 path on Tempo and the fused interpreter on BNB Smart Chain, which the init code probes do not reach. A network whose result differs by one unit in the swapper's favour would let pools pay out more than they hold.

leads.question: On Tempo a write to an empty slot costs 250,000 gas and one transaction may use 30,000,000. What does one swap step cost when it crosses an initialized tick whose two fee growth slots are written for the first time, how many such crossings fit in one transaction, and what does it cost an ordinary account to initialize that many ticks with dust positions around the price of the largest pool? Does a removal of liquidity ever write an empty slot?
leads.why: The L3 profile has no gas figure. At 500,000 gas for the two fee growth slots alone, about sixty first time crossings fill a transaction, so dust positions can force a large trade into many transactions (src/libraries/Pool.sol swap loop and tick crossing). Removal of liquidity touches two ticks and should stay possible, which the measurement would confirm.

attempts.answer: Measured by simulation at block 50,363,527. A first crossing of a tick with both fee growth outside slots empty costs 504,684 gas, with one slot empty about 254,500 gas. 58 such crossings fit in the 30,000,000 gas of one transaction. A dust position on a fresh tick costs about 540,000 gas, which is 0.0003 USD at the base fee floor. A removal of liquidity can write two empty slots, the fee growth inside values of the position, about 500,000 gas, and never crosses ticks, so it stays possible. Filed as a low finding with effect degrade.

leads.question: Do transactions that call the PoolManager on Tempo count against mainBlockGeneralGasLimit, which block 50,314,865 reports as 30,000,000 against a block gasLimit of 500,000,000? Is the base fee of 600,000,000 per gas fixed by the protocol, and does a proposer order transactions inside the general limit by tip or by arrival? What does it cost per day to fill the general limit of every block with cheap transactions?
leads.why: At the base fee seen in 1,024 consecutive blocks, 30,000,000 gas costs 0.018 dollars per block, and blocks arrive about every 0.54 seconds, which is under 3,000 dollars per day if the fee does not rise with use. Every exit from the PoolManager is a call to unlock (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114) and would compete for that limit. If ordering is by arrival, or the fee is fixed, an ordinary account could hold liquidity providers out for as long as it pays. The stablecoin unit did not look at fee dynamics.

attempts.answer: PoolManager transactions count against the general limit: the payload builder defers a transaction that is not a payment once 30,000,000 general gas is used. The base fee is no longer fixed. Since T7 it follows the EIP-1559 formula against a 10,000,000 gas target between 600,000,000 and 12,000,000,000 attodollars, so the 600,000,000 seen in 1,024 blocks is the floor of a quiet chain. Ordering is by tip. Filling the general lane costs 0.018 USD per block at the floor and 0.36 USD at the cap, about 57,600 USD per day at the cap, and a withdrawal that outbids the filler's tip is included first.

leads.question: Does the execution client of each of these OP Stack chains contain a rule that turns a user deposit into a failed deposit or leaves it out, as intercept_blacklisted_deposit does in the X Layer client? Search the handler and block executor of base/node, world-chain, celo-kona, mega-evm and the Conduit builds for calls made before a deposit executes.
leads.why: Forced inclusion through the L1 portal is the mitigation that every operator filtering finding on these chains relies on (F-017, F-030). On X Layer it turned out to be voidable at the execution layer. Soneium already restricts listed contracts at its RPC and sequencer and nobody read its execution client for the same rule.

attempts.answer: MegaETH part. mega-evm has no rule that fails or drops a deposit because of its sender or target. before_run handles only transactions from the system address, and the block executor sends deposits through the general limiter with an exemption from the data availability tests. A deposit fails only on resource limits that apply to its own execution. The closed mega-reth payload builder was not read. The other chains of this lead belong to other units.

leads.question: Do the B20 precompile on Base, the CAS20 dispatcher in the Jenner client and the Robinhood stock tokens have any path on which transfer returns true while the amount is credited to an account other than the named recipient or held by a guard contract, as TIP-20 does on Tempo for a recipient whose receive policy rejects the sender? Who names the account that can recover such funds?
leads.why: F-033 shows that on Tempo a payout can succeed for the PoolManager and never reach the recipient (src/types/Currency.sol:60-75 accepts a true word). OUSD exists on Base and on Tempo under the same policy administrator. If a recipient side policy on another chain can be set by a third party for a router or a wallet, payouts to it are diverted with no failed call to warn the user.

attempts.answer: BNB Smart Chain part: the CAS20 code has no path on which transfer returns true while the amount is credited elsewhere. A receiver or sender policy failure reverts the transfer with PolicyForbids, and a success writes the source and the named recipient only. No guard contract and no recovery account exist in the design. The Base and Robinhood Chain parts belong to other units and were not examined.

leads.question: Settle the two plausible HyperEVM items with one fact: when a treasury deployer names an EVM address as AQAv2 treasury, must that address sign a message, send a CoreWriter action or hold a HyperCore account first? Read the HyperCore action schema for the designation and look for a designation whose treasury address is a contract.
leads.why: F-020 and the new AQAv2 finding stay plausible on this point alone. If no consent is required, unsigned system transfers can move an ERC-20 balance out of a contract that never called transfer, which breaks assumption A2 for the PoolManager and changes the actor from operator to whoever can pass the stake and vote conditions.

attempts.answer: Same fact as L-180: no signature, CoreWriter action or HyperCore account of the named address preceded the system transfers. The node also sends transfers in the name of the CoreDepositWallet, a contract, so a contract address can be the sender of a system transaction. I found no second AQAv2 token, so there is no example of a designation whose treasury address is a contract. The actor stays operator, because activation needs a validator vote and two deployers with 500,000 HYPE staked each.

leads.question: Settle F-024 with one fact: is the risk control filter of the block builder switched on for the X Layer mainnet sequencer, and has any source hash been written to the deposit blacklist at 0x59055c0ef0be92018b33f877a3eB816355791727? An indexer with full log access for that contract answers the second part.
leads.why: F-024 is plausible because the filter state on mainnet is unknown, and the new high finding on voided deposits rests on source at one tag. Both verdicts depend on whether the rules are in use.

attempts.answer: Operator only hazard. Second part answered: the blacklist stores no source hash and no operator at block 76,668,710. First part still open: the filter flag of the mainnet sequencer is a start parameter that no public interface exposes, the release notes do not mention it, and I found no operator statement. F-024 is reported again with the evidence of this cycle.
Operator level. The mainnet filter flag is still not observable from public interfaces.

leads.question: Without comparing code, does the Unichain predeploy behave as src/PoolManager.sol says? With a caller contract placed by state override, check by eth_call: settle with value after sync of a token reverts with NonzeroNativeValue, settle after sync(address(0)) credits msg.value, a settle without payment credits zero, take reverts while locked, clear accepts only the exact positive delta, mint and burn move the delta and the claim by the same amount, and collectProtocolFees for a synced token reverts.
leads.why: Every Unichain clearance assumes src/ describes a contract of a different size that was placed at genesis. A behaviour test is the method the owner has not ruled out. A missing native value guard there would matter less than on Celo because ETH has no ERC-20 face on Unichain, yet the other checks cover the accounting of every pool on that chain.

attempts.answer: Ran the behaviour test on the Unichain predeploy and on the other 20 PoolManagers with a stub placed by state override. Unichain at blocks 64690717, 64690913 and 64691062 gave the same words as Ethereum: NonzeroNativeValue for settle with value after a token sync, a credit of msg.value after sync(address(0)), zero for a settle without payment, ManagerLocked for take, settle, settleFor, clear, mint and burn while locked, MustClearExactPositiveDelta for a clear that is not exact, mint and burn moving the delta and the claim by the same amount, CurrencyNotSettled for an unpaid mint, the lock closed after unlock returns and the synced currency reset by settle. Not tested on Unichain: the synced currency guard of collectProtocolFees, because the fee controller there is the zero address.

leads.question: On Celo and Arc, read the deployed Universal Router and PositionManager: do they call sync(address(0)) before every native settle, do they ever treat the CELO token or 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 as the wrapped native currency, and what do they do with a route that names both address(0) and the token face of the same balance?
leads.why: The two chains are the only ones where the native asset has a transferable ERC-20 face, so they are where the guard at src/PoolManager.sol:356 and the comment at line 348 matter. The settlement model cleared core. The periphery that ordinary users go through was not read on either chain, and a router that settles the face with msg.value or skips the sync leaves its users with reverts or with funds credited to nobody.

attempts.answer: Arc half answered and safe, Celo half not examined by this unit. On Arc the Universal Router, Universal Router 2.1.2 and PositionManager sync address(0) before every native settle that the SETTLE action makes, never treat 0x3600 as wrapped native (their WETH9 immutable is a contract that reverts on every call), and handle a route that names both ids as two currencies. Paying the wrong id ends in CurrencyNotSettled.

First question answered for both networks: the deployed Universal Routers and PositionManagers on Celo and Arc call sync(address(0)) before every native settle (verified source for the 2.1.x routers, code match for the others). The questions about the wrapped native setting and about routes that name both faces were not examined in this unit.

Celo half. The PositionManager (WETH9() and constructor argument) and the first Universal Router (constructor argument weth9) name the CELO token 0x471EcE3750Da237f93B8E339c536989b8978a438 as wrapped native. Universal Router 2.1.1 and 2.1.2 name 0x5Dc88340E1c5c6366864Ee415d6034cadd1A9897, a contract that reverts on every call. deposit() and withdraw(uint256) revert on the CELO token, so wrap and unwrap actions revert. All three verified sources call sync before every settle (DeltaResolver.sol lines 38 to 48). A route that names both address(0) and the CELO token is two currencies to the periphery and to core. Each is settled under its own id, the CELO token id can be paid from native value the periphery holds, and a mistake ends in CurrencyNotSettled. No path credits value to nobody.

leads.question: The Elysium bridge contract on HyperEVM holds 298,480 HYPE and executes child chain messages as calls made by itself. What happens when an Elysium account sends a message whose target is the HYPE bridge address 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222, a token system address or CoreWriter: is a HyperCore balance credited to the bridge contract, and can a later message spend it?
leads.why: The arbitrum-family unit left this open. The backing of every bridged asset on Elysium, including the HYPE and USDC that its PoolManager holds, sits in that contract. An ordinary Elysium account that can move the backing into a HyperCore account leaves holders of the bridged tokens, pools included, unable to withdraw to HyperEVM.

attempts.answer: A simulated executeCall from the Elysium outbox shows that the Bridge sends HYPE to 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 and calls CoreWriter without restriction, and both name the Bridge itself as the HyperCore user. A later message could spend that HyperCore account. The escrowed 297,189 HYPE is not reachable this way, because the Bridge sends only the value of a message and that value was burned on Elysium. No such message has been executed and the Bridge has no HyperCore account. The gateway that holds bridged tokens was not read in this cycle.

leads.question: Which go-ethereum commit do the sequencers of the three Nitro chains run (the endpoint reports nitro v3.13.0-rc.9 while the source was read at v3.11.3), and does EVM.Call in that commit keep the balance check for every caller, as the critic saw in OffchainLabs/go-ethereum master, where isSystemCall is used for witness gas only?
leads.why: The source reading of this unit is two releases behind the running build. Upstream go-ethereum now skips the value transfer for the system caller, and a merge of that change into Nitro would need a second look at which ArbOS paths use that caller.

leads.question: Is collect on the Arc fee controller (3,480 bytes at 0x2f2bd3f43880b9644211f16d861b0672aab23782) open to any caller, where does it send native USDC, and can the destination pay it back to the PoolManager inside the same transaction?
leads.why: collectProtocolFees exempts address(0) from the synced currency test with the remark that native settle uses msg.value (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). On Arc and Celo the native balance is also what balanceOf of the token face reports, so a native collection moves the figure that a pending settle of the face will read. The settlement model allowed a withdrawal at any point and found no gain. It did not model a destination that returns the funds.

leads.question: Where is the opcode fusion code of pull request 3395 in the BNB Smart Chain client that validators run, which opcode sequences does it fuse, and which sequences caused the bad block fixed by pull requests 3582 and 3584?
leads.why: The established L1 unit could not find the feature in the five files it read. An interpreter that rewrites bytecode has already produced one consensus fault on this chain, and the PoolManager bytecode is optimizer output with long stack sequences.

leads.question: After T14 activates on 2026-12-08, what does 0xAACC000000000000000000000000000000000000 answer to the PoolManager call shapes, and can an account of the new configurable type be the sender of a transaction whose address was fixed before its code or configuration existed?
leads.why: The address is codeless today and returns success to every call. Assumption A7 and the hook address rule depend on code at an address staying what it was, and a new account type is a new way for behaviour at a fixed address to change.

leads.question: From Blockscout or another indexer, what are the twenty largest token balances of the PoolManager on Soneium, Ink, Zora and World Chain, and which of them rebase, answer at a second address, or have a block list or pause role?
leads.why: The four chains have no L3 record of their own. The issuer finding F-028 lists three of them by analogy.

leads.question: In the parallel executors of Bor (BlockSTM), World Chain (flashblocks validation with block access lists) and Monad (optimistic execution with retries), is a transaction that is re-executed after a conflict always started with an empty transient map, and is the transient map of a discarded attempt ever merged into the state the next transaction reads?
leads.why: Three units cleared A1 from the serial path or from the per transaction state object and each noted that the merge step was not read to the end. The synced currency and reserves are the only PoolManager state that can outlive a call (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32), and a stale pair from a discarded attempt would be read by settle as real.

leads.question: Who controls the hooks that most new pools use, 0x4e3468951d49f2eea976ed0d6e75ffcb44a9a544 and 0x2c668601193e4a081dd82604785e436aff6a2acc on Robinhood Chain and 0x6b1216a40b65c83e9c9e18a562c446697b8cf8ec on Elysium, and what can the owner of each change after pools exist: fees taken through the swap return deltas, a pause, or the code behind the address.
leads.why: A third of the sampled pools on Robinhood Chain and four fifths on Elysium share one hook. The Robinhood hook carries the afterRemoveLiquidity flag, so F-004 applies to every one of its pools at once. The Elysium hook has an owner and takes swap deltas. This is a pool-creator matter, and it decides how much of the liquidity on these chains sits behind a single contract.

attempts.answer: Pool-creator level hook ownership. Not worked this cycle, whose scope excludes hook sweeps.

leads.question: Which contracts carry the 26 activated Stylus code hashes on Robinhood Chain, and is any of them, or a copy, the hook or a currency of an initialized pool.
leads.why: F-003 now lists Robinhood Chain. Its impact there depends on whether any pool uses a Stylus program. The Initialize logs and the program addresses in the ProgramActivated logs can be joined by an indexer.

leads.question: What does the unpublished build v3.13.0-rc.9 at commit b72783f change against v3.12.4 in the sequencer side filters and in RPC behaviour.
leads.why: The consensus rules are fixed by the consensus-v61 module root, so execution results cannot differ. Sequencer policy can. On Robinhood Chain the address filter and its neighbour effects decide which transactions are accepted, and this cycle could read them only at v3.12.4.

leads.question: When an ArbOS version with Amsterdam rules is scheduled, which transaction types can have the system address 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe as sender or caller, and does evm.Call then let its frames carry value without a balance debit.
leads.why: The fork already contains the branch that skips the balance check and the transfer for that caller and holds it back until Amsterdam. On Nitro chains the sender of an unsigned parent chain message is the parent chain sender plus a fixed offset, so the system address corresponds to parent chain address 0xeeeeffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffeeed. Nobody is known to control it, and a sender without code cannot receive the unlock callback, so I see no path today. The question should be asked again when the version is scheduled.

leads.question: Can a HyperCore spot deployer link a token to the Elysium Bridge, an Elysium gateway or the Outbox on HyperEVM by making that contract send the finalize EVM contract action through CoreWriter, and what do HyperCore system transactions then call on it.
leads.why: Any Elysium account can make the Bridge call CoreWriter with data of its choice. This cycle reasoned that a linked Bridge neither answers transfer nor emits Transfer events and did not test it. The Bridge holds the HYPE that backs the PoolManager's native balance on Elysium.

leads.question: Does the compiled PoolManager, driven through the test routers of src/test on a local chain, give the same deltas, events and revert data as the Python transcription on the cases this unit replayed, in particular the 20,000 hook delta runs of test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:160-266 and the 8,920 cases of the differential against test/bin/v3Factory.bytecode?
leads.why: The transcription follows the source text of PoolManager.sol and Hooks.sol. It cannot show a difference introduced by the compiler, by the via_ir optimiser or by the assembly that copies and parses hook return data, and those parts decide which account is debited. Lead L-024 asks the same for the math libraries only. The check needs forge and nothing outside this repository.

leads.question: Does a build of src/ with the settings in foundry.toml (solc 0.8.26, via_ir, 44444444 optimizer runs, cancun, bytecode_hash none) give a PoolManager runtime of 24009 bytes and the creation code hash 19281018184167079101887460999643277467915809731640262058315305465805214934776 recorded in snapshots/PoolManagerTest.json, and does forge test --isolate reproduce the gas values in snapshots/ without a diff?
leads.why: The creation code hash is the one witness inside the repository that covers every line of src/ at once. A different hash would show that the source text changed after the snapshots were written, and the gas diff would point at the function. This unit could only check the snapshots for plausibility because forge and solc are not installed and nothing may be installed. The check uses only files of this repository.

leads.question: Does test_fuzz_swap in test/libraries/Pool.t.sol pass under the fixed fuzz seed 0x4444 with 1000 runs, or does it reach a zero amountSpecified with a 100 percent swap fee, where line 129 expects InvalidFeeForExactOut and Pool.sol:311-320 returns without a revert?
leads.why: If the committed test fails against the committed source, one of the two was edited after the other, and the comparison operator at Pool.sol:313 would be the place to look. The zero amount path itself changes no state, so the question is about the history of the file and has no direct fund effect.

leads.question: Do several thousand mined Swap, ModifyLiquidity and Donate events per network reproduce from the pool state at the block before, when replayed with a transcription of src/libraries/Pool.sol fed through extsload, including swaps that cross many initialized ticks?
leads.why: This verifier reproduced 107 mined swaps on 20 networks and 370 Quoter quotes on 21 networks with no difference, six mined swaps per network or fewer. HyperEVM returned no PoolManager log in the scanned range and has no mined sample. Monad compiles hot bytecode, BNB Smart Chain has an opcode fusion interpreter, Tempo pins a JIT crate and the Arc release in use is unknown, so a larger sample of mined results on these chains would close the cycle 2 critic gap on execution paths that an eth_call may not take. The method is read only and needs no contract.

attempts.answer: For chain 999: the whole mined history was replayed in cycles 10, 13 and 14 (2,284 swaps and 56 removals, every one matching), and cycle 15 checked 33,760 v3 style swaps of the validator; since the cycle 14 head the PoolManager logged only 19 Initialize events and no Swap, ModifyLiquidity or Donate. The other chains of this lead belong to other units.

leads.question: While the PoolManager is on the G$ block list, does a Superfluid distribution or stream to it raise balanceOf(PoolManager) so that sync and settle credit the payer, and does GoodDollar plan to use adminBurn on the PoolManager's 550,022,104 G$?
leads.why: A credit through agreements would let G$ be sold into the frozen pools while liquidity providers cannot withdraw G$. A burn would leave G$ pool liquidity and G$ claims without backing. The first part needs a simulation with an unlock caller, which this unit did not build.

leads.question: Which contracts are allowedWrappers of the permissioned wrapper tokens on X Layer, and can a user of one of them call wrapToPoolManager for an amount that is covered by underlying tokens already sitting in the wrapper instead of tokens the user paid?
leads.why: A take that names the wrapper as recipient burns wrapper tokens and leaves the underlying in the wrapper. If an allowed router mints against that surplus for the next user, the wrapper supply in the PoolManager can be refilled without payment. The pools are small today (2,000 to 4,000 USD each).

leads.question: What do the values returned by globalTransferSettings() on USDG (1771954688, 86400, 0, 0) limit, and can the issuer use them to cap transfers out of one address per day?
leads.why: A transfer cap on the PoolManager address would make takes of USDG revert once the cap is used, which blocks withdrawals from the 879,000 USD USDG/USDT0 pool without a freeze entry.

leads.question: Which execution client produces Celo mainnet blocks, and do celo-org/op-geth and celo-kona agree on whether transient storage written by debitGasFees is still present in the main call? In op-geth Prepare runs before the debit and nothing clears afterwards, and celo-kona clears after the debit.
leads.why: The two clients would disagree for a fee currency that leaves a transient value behind. The PoolManager is not a fee currency and no registered fee currency is known to call it, so the reach to pool funds is small. The clearance of assumption A1 on Celo should rest on the client that builds blocks.

leads.question: Can a G$ position held through the Celo PositionManager be reduced so that the paired currency leaves while the G$ delta is moved into another position in the same unlock, and how much of the paired currencies do the G$ pools hold?
leads.why: The PositionManager code has no call to PoolManager.mint, so the G$ side of a removal cannot become a claim. If the delta cannot be moved into another position either, a liquidity provider must forfeit the G$ with clear to withdraw the paired currency while the issuer block lasts. This sizes the frozen value of finding 0 and does not change its actor.

leads.question: On an archive node, compare the balance of 0x2222222222222222222222222222222222222222 and of the recipient before and after a block that holds a HYPE system transaction, and read what the node does when the recipient reverts.
leads.why: The validator node is closed source. The public clients debit the bridge address, and an observed state diff would confirm that no HYPE is created on the EVM side without a HyperCore debit. The public RPC serves latest state for old blocks, so this needs an archive endpoint.

attempts.answer: Done on two archive endpoints. In four blocks with one HYPE system transfer each, the bridge address lost exactly the transferred value and the recipient gained it, so no HYPE is created on the EVM side. The second half of the lead is open: all 46 observed transfers went to accounts without code, so the node's behaviour for a reverting recipient was not seen. A simulated transfer of this shape to the PoolManager reverts.

leads.question: After the Jenner fork on 2026-12-08, does any new system call or transaction type on BNB Smart Chain run user-chosen code with caller 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe and nonzero value, and does the probe from this unit still return the same words?
leads.why: The client reports a value that nobody paid for that caller. The PoolManager credits msg.value without reading a balance (src/PoolManager.sol:352-354), so one reachable frame of that kind would expose every BNB pool.

attempts.answer: Jenner adds no system call and no transaction type. The client still makes three calls from 0xfffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffe, each with zero value and a fixed target, Parlia sends system messages from the coinbase, and the CAS20 and payment lane code run no contract. The probe returned the same words on Chapel with Jenner active (CALLVALUE 7, no balance moved) and on mainnet. The reth-bsc client moves the value for that caller, a disagreement on a call that no transaction can produce.

leads.question: Which go-ethereum, op-geth and Celo releases contain the system caller rule, and does any sequencer or validator of these chains run one of them as its execution client?
leads.why: The rule is in the source of three clients and was observed on one endpoint only. The public endpoints of the OP Stack chains run op-reth and the Celo endpoint runs an older build, so the running behaviour of other nodes is not shown by this unit's probes.

leads.question: Does Monad burn the balance of a contract that executes SELFDESTRUCT with itself as beneficiary when the contract was not created in the same transaction, or is the zero balance seen in the probe an effect of the state override?
leads.why: Ethereum keeps the balance in that case. A burn rule would be an undocumented opcode difference. It does not reach the PoolManager, whose bytecode has no SELFDESTRUCT, and it would matter to hooks or tokens that use the opcode.

leads.question: Does any account in Tempo's genesis or state hold a nonzero native balance at the EVM level?
leads.why: The interpreter moves value normally when a balance exists. The native branch of settle and take is inert only while no account holds one. A funded account that delegates with EIP-7702 could make inner calls with value even though the transaction itself must carry none.

leads.question: forno.celo.org answers from a reth based client (reth/v2.2.0-74cc8bb) and from a Geth build (c7ed55b8 of 2026-08-17).
