leads.question: In bor v2.12.0-beta, find the definition of keccakResultCache (used at core/vm/interpreter.go:62 and core/vm/instructions.go:313-330) and of the result caches that the import prefetcher and the parallel V2 workers share. Is the key the full input bytes copied out of EVM memory, or the slice returned by scope.Memory.GetPtr, or a fingerprint of the input? Can an entry written by a speculative execution that BlockSTM later aborts be read by another worker? Which bor release first ships this code, and does Polygon's validator configuration set EnablePrecompileCache?
leads.why: Every pool id (a keccak over the 160 byte PoolKey) and every position key (58 bytes, src/libraries/Position.sol) would go through this cache. A key that aliases memory or is a fingerprint lets one input return the hash of another. That would give a wrong storage slot for a pool, a position or a claim balance on a path that any account drives with chosen calldata. The 64 byte path copies its key into a [64]byte array (instructions.go:270-272); the widened path passes data straight to Load and Store.

attempts.answer: Read on 2026-11-25 in 0xPolygon/bor at tag v2.12.0-beta (core/vm/instructions.go 258-330, interpreter.go 50-71, shared_cache.go, bounded_cache.go, keccak_cache.go). The widened cache keccakResultCache is a sync.Map from string(data) to common.Hash. Store copies the input (string(data)), so a stored key never points into EVM memory, and it takes the hash by value. Load builds a string view of memory without a copy, which sync.Map.Load compares and does not keep, and the calling goroutine owns that memory for the length of the call. The key is the full input, with no fingerprint, so inputs of different lengths or contents cannot share an entry. An entry written by a speculative execution that BlockSTM later discards is still keccak of its own key, since the hash is computed from the same bytes immediately before Store. On a miss the handler falls through to the ordinary path with the freshly computed hash. The cache exists only when a node sets the precompile cache flag (default false) and is dropped at the end of each block. The legacy path for 64 byte inputs, which v2.11.1 already has, copies the key into a [64]byte array. A standalone copy of the Load and Store logic (cycles/016/own-check.work/keccak_cache/main.go, sha256 standing in for keccak) was run with 16 goroutines on inputs of 58 and 160 bytes that differ in one byte, in buffers overwritten after every call: 12,800,000 lookups, 4,809,737 hits, 0 wrong, every stored key still maps to the hash of its own bytes, and a shorter run under the Go race detector reports no race. v2.12.0-beta is the only tag with this code; v2.12.0 does not exist yet and Polygon's endpoint reports v2.11.1. Whether Polygon's validators will set the flag is not known and does not matter for correctness as read. L-664 and L-668 keep the rerun of the opcode checks against a v2.12 node.

leads.question: On the C-Chain today, can any transaction an ordinary account sends write a multicoin balance into the PoolManager's account storage (AddBalanceMultiCoin through an atomic import, or the NativeAssetCall and NativeAssetBalance precompiles at 0x0100000000000000000000000000000000000002 and 0x...0001)? attempts.answer: No transaction an ordinary account can send today writes an asset balance into the PoolManager account. At avalanchego 1.15.3 (endpoint commit 983815fd) the only writers are non-AVAX import and export outputs, which sanityCheck rejects with no fork gate in the txpool and in block re-verification, and NativeAssetCall, which reverts from Banff on; the precompiles at 0x01..01 and 0x01..02 revert by eth_call from the PoolManager and from a plain address, and the old opcodes 0xcd and 0xcf are undefined. Even a write would be harmless, because the EVM key set (bit 0 of byte 0 cleared) and the asset key set (bit set) are disjoint. The held X-chain asset flag changes only the emptiness test, which does not apply to an account with code. eth_getProof is not served by any reachable public endpoint, so the PoolManager trie itself was not inspected. F-040 should say that the fold comes from the key hook that keeps EVM keys out of the asset partition, that the partition has had no writer open to the public since Banff (October 2022), and that the fold, not the asset partition, is the only part with any effect on contracts.

leads.question: Under the SAE executor of avalanchego 1.15.3, what state does eth_call at latest, at safe and at a block number run against: the last accepted block before its execution, or the last settled state? attempts.answer: eth_call, eth_getStorageAt, eth_getBalance and debug_traceCall run against the post-execution state of the resolved block: latest is the last executed block, safe and finalized the last settled, pending the last executed under the C-Chain default, and an explicit number up to the accepted tip waits for execution. A transaction of an accepted block always runs, in block order, on the state left by the one before; the worst-case check guarantees only that it can pay, and any non-revert error halts the node instead of skipping it. Transient storage is replaced per transaction. Only BASEFEE and the effective gas price can be lower than the header says. No path leaves an unlock half applied. Inside the callback do a take of an ERC-20 and of native USDC, a settle, a swap and an ERC-6909 mint, and a nested Multicall3From call from the callback. Choose the outer gas so that the child returns success and complete_subcall then runs out of gas (evm.rs 1186-1196). After the precompile reports failure, are every PoolManager slot (slot0, liquidity, ticks, positions, ERC-6909 balances), every token balance, the native balance, the 0x3600 face and the transient Lock, delta and count slots back to their values before the subcall?

If it restored PoolManager storage but kept a token transfer, or restored the debit but not the payout, an ordinary account could keep a take whose debt was rolled back, which drains any pool on Arc. Settlement relies on all of src/PoolManager.sol:104-114 and 291-297 reverting together.

leads.question: Using the mega-evm and SALT sources that F-105 cites, at what bucket multiplier does one zero to nonzero SSTORE cost more than the per-transaction gas limit, the per-transaction storage gas or state growth limit, or the block limits that apply to transactions sent through the sequencer, and what does an ordinary account pay to grow one bucket that far under the 80 percent doubling rule? Is there any cap on bucket growth or any shrink rule that runs without the operator?
leads.why: F-105 stops at the L1 exit, which closes at multiplier 64 for about 0.003 ETH. Position.update writes two fee growth slots on every liquidity change (src/libraries/Position.sol:99-100), and a first token balance or a new tick is also a zero to nonzero write. If the sequencer limit can be reached at a cost below the value of the targeted positions, an ordinary account can freeze chosen LP positions on MegaETH for good, which is an in-scope freeze.

attempts.answer: Answered in cycle 20 (theme-mined-gas-cap, recorded in state/cleared.json): user transactions with 984,000,000 gas were mined in MegaETH blocks 32,838,613 to 32,838,912, so the sequencer's cap per transaction is at least that. Under the rule F-105 records (storage gas of 20,000 times the multiplier minus 1 for a zero to non-zero write, a bucket doubling at 80 percent use), the two fresh writes of a removal exceed that cap only at multiplier 32,768, which takes about 3.36 million entries in one bucket and about 7.3e14 gas, about 733 ETH at the base fee floor. The MegaETH PoolManager holds about 17,000 dollars, so freezing a position through the sequencer path is far from paying. F-105 stays as recorded: the L1 exit closes at multiplier 64 for about 0.003 ETH, and needs the sequencer to refuse the provider. L-1332 sizes which positions that concerns.

leads.question: For the 137 PoolManager positions with liquidity on MegaETH, which ones need a zero to nonzero write on their next removal through the sequencer (fee growth slots, a recipient's first token balance, an ERC-6909 first balance) and which can avoid it, and what share of the PoolManager's value sits in those that cannot?

A producer that specialises per contract would leave the PoolManager's own wide branch untested, and a wrong result there changes the input left after fees in src/libraries/SwapMath.sol for every pool.

leads.question: In arc-node v0.8.6, does the subcall continuation map keyed by frame depth (evm.rs 217-218, 1081-1090, 757-758) stay correct when a child at depth d+1 makes its own CallFrom subcall through a 7702 delegated tx.origin, when the child halts with CallTooDeep, and when an inspector is attached as on the tracing node? theme-celo-xlayer-arc-journal-lift ran the frame journal of arc-node v0.8.6 (1,062 sequences) but not the second revert protocol that the subcall precompile uses. In crates/evm/src/evm.rs at v0.8.6 (fetched by the critic), init_subcall takes checkpoint() and at once checkpoint_commit() (lines 1052-1053), and complete_subcall rolls back a child that succeeded through revert_subcall_checkpoint, a dummy checkpoint followed by checkpoint_revert(saved_cp) (lines 1249-1259), when completion accounting runs out of gas (1186-1196) or completion fails (1226-1228). The cleared items on CallFrom read the main branch for sender spoofing and transient sharing only; none ran the rollback with PoolManager state inside the child. The verifier of the theme raised the same question at medium.

Separately, the evm2 revision 7c9f3b6 that Tempo pins carries an entry for a transaction dispatched from inside a running one (suspended_frames, enclosing_refund, ExecutionGuard in evm/mod.rs, cycle 32 critic). OPCODES.md says no Tempo code calls it today, but no unit has read what it does with transient storage and the journal, so its effect on A1 is unknown before T15 is tagged.

An earlier clearance of Tempo's native branch said the zero balance was confirmed for probe accounts and not for every genesis account. The critic fetched crates/chainspec/src/genesis/presto.json from tempoxyz/tempo main (chainId 4217, the file PRESTO loads in crates/chainspec/src/spec.rs:140-142): 14 alloc entries, none with a nonzero balance. eth_getProof on rpc.mainnet.tempo.xyz returns balance 0x0 for the PoolManager 0x33620f62…7029, for address 0x0 and for 0xfeec…0000, while eth_getBalance answers the 0x4242… placeholder. The placeholder is an RPC answer, not trie state. What is still unread is whether any system call or precompile on Tempo credits a native balance after genesis.
